## New words

{{< glossary position coordinate axis x-axis y-axis z-axis origin 2d 3d negative-number >}}

## 1. Math is inside every game

Open any mobile game. You see things move, turn, and appear.
Behind every one of these, there is math.

| In the game… | The math | We learn it in… |
|---|---|---|
| The player walks to a coin. | position and vectors | weeks 1–3 |
| A cannon turns to aim. | angles (trigonometry) | week 4 |
| A character grows or spins. | transformations (matrices) | weeks 5–7 |
| "If health is 0, game over." | logic | weeks 9–10 |
| A chest gives a random prize. | probability | weeks 11–13 |

The computer must answer these questions many times every second.
It does this with math.

Today we start with the first question in every game:
**where is everything?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 1"}
Match each game moment with its math. You can use an answer more than once.

::: {.match}
An enemy drops a rare sword only 1 time in 20.
:   probability

The car is 5 steps to the right of the start.
:   position

The door opens only if you have the key.
:   logic

The tower turns to face the enemy.
:   angle

The hero grows two times bigger after a power-up.
:   transformation

A spin wheel gives a random prize.
:   probability
:::
:::

## 2. Every object has a position

The computer does not see the screen like you.
It only knows numbers.

So each object has a **position**.
In a flat (**2D**) game, a position is two numbers.

![A 2D game world. The player is at (3, 2). A coin is at (7, 4).](sims/grid-position.png){width=85%}

- The red line is the **x-axis**. It goes from left to right. x grows to the **right**.
- The green line is the **y-axis**. It goes from down to up. y grows **up**.
- The corner where they meet is the **origin**. There, x = 0 and y = 0.

Each axis is like a ruler. The numbers show the steps from the origin.

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 2"}
Look at the picture above (the grid with the player and the coin).

::: {.match extra="0|the origin"}
What number is at the right end of the x-axis?
:   10

What number is at the top of the y-axis?
:   6

Which axis goes from left to right?
:   the x-axis

Which axis goes from down to up?
:   the y-axis
:::
:::

## 3. Write a position: (x, y)

We write a 2D position like this: **(x, y)**.
Each number is a **coordinate**.

- First number: **x**. Count to the right.
- Second number: **y**. Count up.

The player is at **(3, 2)**: 3 steps right, 2 steps up.

::: {.callout-note title="Example: find the position of the coin"}
1. Start at the origin, (0, 0).
2. Count the steps right to the coin: 7. So **x = 7**.
3. Count the steps up to the coin: 4. So **y = 4**.
4. Write x first, then y: the coin is at **(7, 4)**.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Watch out!"}
Order is important! (3, 2) and (2, 3) are **different** places.
Always write **x first**, then y.
:::

Some points are on an axis:

- y = 0: the point is **on the x-axis**. Example: (6, 0).
- x = 0: the point is **on the y-axis**. Example: (0, 2).

Now try it. Move the player. Then press **Challenge** and catch the coin.

{{< sim file="sims/grid-position.html" poster="sims/grid-position.png" title="Move the player with x and y" height="500" >}}

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 3"}
Look at this picture. It does not change (the simulator does).

![The player is at (3, 2). Where is the coin?](sims/grid-position.png){width=70%}

::: {.match extra="(4, 7)|(3, 2)|the axis"}
Where is the coin in this picture?
:   (7, 4)

In the simulator, move the player to (0, 0). What is this point called?
:   the origin

The player is at (3, 2). It moves 4 steps right. What is the new position?
:   (7, 2)
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 4"}
Write the position. Start at the origin each time.

::: {.match extra="(2, 0)|(4, 0)"}
3 steps right, 5 steps up
:   (3, 5)

5 steps right, 3 steps up
:   (5, 3)

6 steps right, 0 steps up
:   (6, 0)

0 steps right, 2 steps up
:   (0, 2)

On the y-axis, 4 steps up
:   (0, 4)
:::
:::

## 4. Moving changes the numbers

When an object moves, its position changes.
But only **one number** changes for each direction.

| The object moves… | This number changes | It gets… |
|---|---|---|
| right | x | bigger (+) |
| left | x | smaller (−) |
| up | y | bigger (+) |
| down | y | smaller (−) |

::: {.callout-note title="Example: move the player"}
The player is at (3, 2).

1. It moves **2 steps left**. x changes: 3 − 2 = 1. Now it is at **(1, 2)**.
2. Then it moves **3 steps up**. y changes: 2 + 3 = 5. Now it is at **(1, 5)**.
:::

What is on the left of the origin? The world does not stop there.
Left of the origin, x is a **negative number** (it has a minus sign).

The player is at (1, 2). It moves 3 steps left: 1 − 3 = −2.
Now the player is at **(−2, 2)**.

In many games, the origin is in the middle of the world.
So negative numbers are normal in game positions.

::: {.callout-note title="Watch out!"}
Left and down make a number **smaller**. It can go below 0.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 5"}
The player is at (5, 3). Find the new position.

::: {.match extra="(3, 3)|(5, 6)"}
It moves 2 steps right.
:   (7, 3)

It moves 3 steps down.
:   (5, 0)

It moves 4 steps left.
:   (1, 3)

It moves 1 step up and 2 steps right.
:   (7, 4)

It moves 7 steps left.
:   (−2, 3)
:::
:::

## 5. From 2D to 3D: add z

Many mobile games are **3D**. The world has depth.
So we need a third number: **z**.

![A 3D position. The player is at (4, 3, 2).](images/axes-3d.png){width=75%}

A 3D position is **(x, y, z)**:

- x → right (left is −)
- y → up (down is −)
- z → forward, into the screen (back is −)

::: {.callout-note title="Example: reach (4, 3, 2)"}
1. Walk **4** steps right. (x = 4)
2. Walk **2** steps forward. (z = 2)
3. Go **3** steps up. (y = 3)

The order of the walk does not matter. The order of the **numbers** does: x, y, z.
:::

Now try it in 3D. Turn the world with your finger. Move the player.
Then press **Challenge** and catch the coin in the air.

{{< sim file="sims/position-3d.html" poster="images/axes-3d.png" title="Move the player in 3D" height="640" >}}

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 6"}
Which number changes: x, y or z? You can use an answer more than once.

::: {.match}
The player walks to the right.
:   x

The player jumps up.
:   y

The player walks forward, into the screen.
:   z

The player falls down.
:   y

The player walks back, out of the screen.
:   z
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 7"}
A 3D player is at (4, 3, 2). Find the new position.

::: {.match extra="(5, 3, 2)|(4, 3, 4)"}
The player jumps up 1.
:   (4, 4, 2)

The player walks forward 5.
:   (4, 3, 7)

The player walks left 4.
:   (0, 3, 2)

The player walks back 2.
:   (4, 3, 0)
:::
:::

## 6. Position in game code

Games are programs. The code must keep the position of every object.
It keeps a 3D position as **three numbers together**: x, y and z.

Here is game code. **Just read it today.**
It is C#, the language of many games (for example, games made with Unity).

```csharp
// a 3D game: the player is at x = 4, y = 3, z = 2
Vector3 playerPosition = new Vector3(4, 3, 2);

// a 2D game: the coin is at x = 7, y = 4
Vector2 coinPosition = new Vector2(7, 4);
```

- `Vector3` means "three numbers together": x, y, z.
- `Vector2` means "two numbers together": x, y. 2D games use it.
- `playerPosition` and `coinPosition` are names. We choose the names.
- The numbers are in the same order as always: **x, y, z**.

You will write code like this later, in *Programming Fundamentals (1)*.

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 8"}
Read the code.

::: {.match extra="4|a 3D position|at the origin"}
`new Vector3(4, 3, 2)`: which number is z?
:   2

`new Vector2(7, 4)`: is this a 2D or a 3D position?
:   a 2D position

`new Vector3(0, 5, 0)`: where is the coin?
:   5 steps up, straight above the origin
:::
:::

## Practice round

Use everything from today. These are a little harder.

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 9 (harder)"}
Find the answer.

::: {.match extra="(4, 0)|(5, 7)|(5, 2, 3)"}
A star is on the x-axis, 2 steps left of the origin. Where is it?
:   (−2, 0)

The player is at (2, 5). It moves 3 steps right and 2 steps down. Where is it now?
:   (5, 3)

A bird is at (1, 2, 3). It flies up 4. Where is it now?
:   (1, 6, 3)

Which point is on the y-axis?
:   (0, 4)
:::
:::

## Class activity {.activity}

**Math hunt: where is the math in a mobile game?** (pairs, about 18 minutes)

1. **Choose** (2 min). Work in pairs. Open one mobile game on one phone.
2. **Hunt** (8 min). Play a little. Find **five moments** where the game uses math.
   Copy this table on paper and fill it.

   | Moment in the game | The math | How do you know? |
   |---|---|---|
   | The coin is above the player. | position | The coin has its own (x, y). |
   | | | |

   For "The math", use: position, angle, transformation, logic or probability.
3. **Think** (3 min). Is your game 2D or 3D? How do you know?
   Find one object that moves. Which number changes when it moves: x, y or z?
4. **Share** (5 min). Tell the class your best moment.
   The teacher writes the math words on the board. Which math is in the most games?

## Summary {.summary}

- Every game uses math. It starts with **position**.
- 2D position: **(x, y)**. 3D position: **(x, y, z)**. Always x first.
- x → right. y ↑ up. z → forward. Left, down and back are **negative** (−).
- The **origin** is (0, 0) in 2D and (0, 0, 0) in 3D.
- When an object moves, only the number for that direction changes.
- In game code: `new Vector2(x, y)` (2D) and `new Vector3(x, y, z)` (3D).
